To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
costly diagnosis and subjective evaluation of treatment success are compatible with the first‐best outcome if the parties have a zero discount rate, or if diagnosis can be separated from treatment.
the first‐ best outcome can always be implemented when the parties’ discount rates are zero, and the set of parameter combinations that allow for the first‐ best is nonempty for any discount rates.
(i) costly diagnosis can be implemented in a first‐best manner if the parties’ patience is infinite, and (ii) costly diagnosis and treatment can always be separated by contracting.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of contracts that are based on a subjective evaluation.
the question of how to implement a first‐best solution if diagnosis is costly and the consumer’s report is subjective.
the role of diagnosis for optimal contracting in the presence of moral hazard and subjective evaluation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the first‐ best solution is implementable if the consumer’s problem can be solved by the high‐ cost treatment in the same period as the diagnosis, and if the discount rates are low enough.
the first‐ best can always be obtained if the parties’ preferences are sufficiently patient.

the first‐ best can always be implemented in the presence of costly and imperfect diagnosis if the parties’ preferences are time separable and if the diagnosis and the treatment can either be provided by one and the same agent or if the diagnosis and treatment can each be contracted out separately.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the first‐ best solution can be obtained in a setting with costly diagnosis, subjective evaluation and moral hazard, but only if the parties’ time discount rates are sufficiently low.
the first‐ best is always implementable if the parties’ preferences are time separable, but that the first‐ and second‐best can differ substantially when the parties have non‐separable preferences.
the consumer’s subjective evaluation is a key to the first‐best outcome.
The main takeaway from our work is that
costly diagnosis can make it difficult to implement the first‐best outcome in a setting with moral hazard, even if the outcome can be made contractible.
the inability of a consumer to observe the outcome of a low‐cost treatment can be a major obstacle to contracting for the optimal treatment of a problem.
costly diagnosis can be used to implement first‐best contracts even when payments cannot depend on objective outcomes.
